title: Role of IL-6 Receptor Signalling on Platelet and RBC Function in Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Formation and Progression
summary:
Beyond their established roles in hemostasis and thrombosis, platelets and erythrocytes have increasingly emerged as key contributors to vascular diseases, particularly in the context of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). AAA is a life-threatening, atherosclerosis-associated vascular disease characterized by a high mortality rate following aneurysm rupture. Its pathophysiology is marked by progressive fragmentation and remodeling of the extracellular matrix, accompanied by chronic inflammation of the aortic wall, ultimately leading to irreversible dilation of the abdominal aorta. Additional pathological hallmarks include inflammatory cell infiltration of the vessel wall, apoptosis of vascular smooth muscle cells, and the formation of a platelet- and erythrocyte-rich intraluminal thrombus (ILT).
Currently, AAA diagnosis relies primarily on ultrasonography, while no disease-modifying pharmacological therapy is available. Consequently, there is an unmet clinical need for targeted therapeutic strategies that address the underlying mechanisms driving AAA progression. The identification of novel platelet- and/or erythrocyte-specific signaling pathways involved in AAA pathogenesis therefore represents a highly relevant area of translational research.
In this context, interleukin-6 (IL-6)-dependent alterations in platelet and erythrocyte function during AAA development may provide important insights into disease mechanisms and facilitate the identification of predictive biomarkers. Circulating inflammatory mediators, including IL-6, are significantly elevated in patients with AAA and positively correlate with aneurysm size. Both experimental and clinical studies have demonstrated a central role of IL-6 signaling in AAA pathophysiology, as reflected by increased circulating levels of IL-6 and soluble IL-6 receptor (sIL-6R) in affected patients. However, pharmacological neutralization of IL-6 does not substantially reduce leukocyte or macrophage infiltration nor does it markedly attenuate aortic wall remodeling. These observations suggest that, in addition to leukocytes, other circulating blood cells —particularly platelets and erythrocytes — may contribute to AAA pathogenesis through IL-6-mediated mechanisms.
We therefore hypothesize that IL-6 promotes platelet–erythrocyte interactions while simultaneously inducing a hyperreactive platelet phenotype. In support of this concept, we and others have demonstrated that enhanced platelet reactivity promotes the formation of platelet–erythrocyte aggregates and increases phosphatidylserine exposure on both cell types. These processes amplify thrombo-inflammatory responses and may accelerate aneurysm progression. Collectively, these mechanisms may contribute to the establishment of a persistent prothrombotic phenotype accompanied by enhanced cellular infiltration into both the intraluminal thrombus and the aortic wall of patients with AAA.
conditions: Abdominal aortic aneurysm, without mention of rupture

interventions.name: Investigation of the AAA-specific pathogenic relevance of IL-6-induced platelet activation states and erythrocyte-associated mechanisms in relation to abdominal aortic aneurysm size and progression.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Individuals presenting for voluntary blood donation at the institutional blood bank who have provided written informed consent for the use of their blood samples for experimental research within the framework of the ATLaNtA study (Study No. 2018-140_2KFogU: Potential Activation Mechanisms and Interactions of Platelets in Degenerative Diseases of the Liver, Brain, and Aorta – ATLaNtA Study).
Patients with an abdominal or thoracic aortic aneurysm (AAA/TAA) scheduled for guideline-based endovascular aneurysm repair (cohort).
Patients with AAA/TAA presenting for routine follow-up examinations at the vascular outpatient clinic.
Patients with other atherosclerotic vascular diseases (excluding AAA/TAA), including peripheral arterial occlusive disease or carotid artery stenosis, presenting for routine follow-up examinations at the vascular outpatient clinic.
Age ≥18 years.
Feasible venous blood collection.
Written informed consent.
Exclusion criteria:
• Absence of written informed consent.
• Psychiatric disorders resulting in impaired decision-making capacity or legal incapacity to provide informed consent.
• Known coagulation disorders.
• Known inherited platelet disorders.
